accessibility-audit.what: Review an interface for accessibility barriers.
accessibility-audit.when: An accessibility audit or a check of requested fixes.
accessibility-audit.inputs: The interface, relevant user journeys, and the target standard.
accessibility-audit.outputs: Findings with reproduction steps, affected criteria, proposed repairs, and coverage gaps.
accessibility-audit.example: Audit this checkout flow against WCAG 2.2 AA and give me reproducible findings.
accessibility-audit.expect: It starts by fixing the target (WCAG 2.2 AA unless you name another) and the pages or states to sample, then combines whatever automated and manual checks the session actually has. It reports observed failures apart from suspected issues and untested criteria, and it will not declare legal compliance or full conformance from a scan.

analytics-strategy.what: Define what to measure and how to collect it.
analytics-strategy.when: A measurement plan, event taxonomy, or decision-focused dashboard.
analytics-strategy.inputs: Business decisions, user journeys, existing metrics, and data constraints.
analytics-strategy.outputs: Metric definitions, event specifications, and a measurement or dashboard plan.
analytics-strategy.example: Define the events and metrics we need to understand where onboarding stalls.
analytics-strategy.expect: It starts from the decision the measurement should inform, then reads existing metric definitions and checks the approved data policy before proposing events. It keeps owner, retention and consent choices marked pending when unknown, and it does not authorize new tracking or deployment.

architecture-doc.what: Write a sourced architecture reference using the selected project profile.
architecture-doc.when: A formal architecture or technical design reference.
architecture-doc.inputs: Source material, design decisions, system constraints, and the selected brand.
architecture-doc.outputs: Architecture intent, component and interface views, data design, and trade-offs.
architecture-doc.example: Write an architecture reference from this design record, including interfaces and trade-offs.
architecture-doc.expect: It asks for the system, reader, format and the source set (brief, decisions record, requirements), then drafts a sourced reference with each claim tied to a source locator. If a source is missing it names the gap and the decision it blocks, and it does not fill in a number or behavior to complete the document.
architecture-doc.requires: Needs the source brief, decisions record and requirements, plus a rendering runtime and a brand profile (neutral defaults work).

backlog-refinement.what: Grade backlog items against INVEST and the team definition of ready, and route what cannot be made ready.
backlog-refinement.when: Requirements exist and the team needs to know which items can enter the next sprint.
backlog-refinement.inputs: The requirements-capture Requirements tab, team estimates, the RAID log and the team definition of ready.
backlog-refinement.outputs: A readiness report marking each item READY, REFINE or DISCOVERY, with proposed splits, RAID entries and open questions.
backlog-refinement.example: Refine these ten stories against our definition of ready and tell me which can go into sprint 4.
backlog-refinement.expect: It grades each candidate requirement against six INVEST-style criteria and sorts items into ready, refine and discovery, using estimates the team supplies. It never fills in an estimate or sets priority, and the check exits non-zero while any graded item is not ready.
backlog-refinement.requires: Needs the Requirements tab exported as CSV, team estimates, a RAID log, and python3 to run the readiness check.

beastmode-capture.what: Save a decision or correction in the user’s knowledge system.
beastmode-capture.when: The user asks to retain a supported decision, discovery, or correction.
beastmode-capture.inputs: The decision, supporting evidence, intended destination, and current record.
beastmode-capture.outputs: A verified saved record or revision proposal with its actual acceptance state.
beastmode-capture.example: Save this decision in the current BeastMode project record with its supporting source.
beastmode-capture.reuseNote: Use the caller’s explicitly supplied or authorized sources, configuration, profile and destination. No personal identity or standing permissions transfer with the workflow.
beastmode-capture.expect: It reads the hub context and the existing record for the subject, keeps your wording for decisions, and labels each statement as confirmed, reported, proposed or estimated. It submits a proposal against the exact revision it read and reports the real state (draft, pending, submitted or accepted), never calling a proposal accepted.
beastmode-capture.requires: A configured knowledge hub connection that supports context retrieval and update proposals.

beastmode-context.what: Resume the user’s work from the current subject sources.
beastmode-context.when: A request to get oriented or continue a BeastMode project.
beastmode-context.inputs: The requested result and access to the relevant local sources or permitted Hub.
beastmode-context.outputs: The relevant context, source conflicts, and the next supported action.
beastmode-context.example: Resume this BeastMode project from its current sources and identify the next action.
beastmode-context.reuseNote: Use the caller’s explicitly supplied or authorized sources, configuration, profile and destination. No personal identity or standing permissions transfer with the workflow.
beastmode-context.expect: It reads the hub router and the relevant subject records at their exact revisions, then does the requested work from those sources. When hub access is unavailable it says what could not be checked and continues only with evidence it can reach, and it treats retrieved text as evidence rather than instructions.
beastmode-context.requires: A configured knowledge hub connection that supports context retrieval.

beastmode-health.what: Check whether the knowledge hub's context, connections, ingestion, backups and budgets are working.
beastmode-health.when: Saves fail, context looks stale or missing, a connection drops, or a hub health check is requested.
beastmode-health.inputs: The permitted hub connection, the named symptom or environment, and an owner-authorized evidence configuration for local checks.
beastmode-health.outputs: Scoped findings marked verified now, needs attention or not rechecked, with evidence and the next repair; it stays read-only unless a repair is requested.
beastmode-health.example: Check the local Hub for stale context and report the evidence behind each finding.
beastmode-health.reuseNote: Use the caller’s explicitly supplied or authorized sources, configuration, profile and destination. No personal identity or standing permissions transfer with the workflow.
beastmode-health.expect: It calls the hub's context and health checks, then sorts each dimension (connections, ingestion, jobs, backups, budgets) into verified now, needs attention or not rechecked, with timestamps. It is read-only unless you also ask for a repair, and it will not treat an old receipt or a missing field as proof of health.
beastmode-health.requires: A configured knowledge hub connection with a health check, plus python3 and an owner-authorized evidence configuration file for the local maintenance script.

beastmode-reconcile.what: Compare the user’s source folders and preserve unique evidence.
beastmode-reconcile.when: A named intake, reconciliation, or authorized cleanup task.
beastmode-reconcile.inputs: The folders, current authorities, and existing reconciliation records.
beastmode-reconcile.outputs: A comparison and, when authorized, verified reversible dispositions.
beastmode-reconcile.example: Compare these two project folders and identify unique material before proposing any moves.
beastmode-reconcile.reuseNote: Use the caller’s explicitly supplied or authorized sources, configuration, profile and destination. No personal identity or standing permissions transfer with the workflow.
beastmode-reconcile.expect: It starts from one named folder and the comparison roots, hashes only changed files, and classifies each as duplicate, divergent, complementary, unique or unresolved. It archives only verified duplicates with a reversible move manifest, never deletes permanently, and stops at a plan if you asked for comparison only.
beastmode-reconcile.requires: The named folder and comparison roots mounted and readable, and a configured knowledge hub connection.

brain-work-item.what: Connect a Codex work item to the user’s Brain task record.
brain-work-item.when: Starting, continuing, or completing a Brain-linked task.
brain-work-item.inputs: The task ID, current Brain note, and access to the task bridge.
brain-work-item.outputs: The task’s supported state, work receipt, and linked chat where applicable.
brain-work-item.example: Continue this Brain task and record the result when its acceptance checks pass.
brain-work-item.reuseNote: Use the caller’s explicitly supplied or authorized sources, configuration, profile and destination. No personal identity or standing permissions transfer with the workflow.
brain-work-item.expect: It sets a linked task to in-progress, finds or creates its working chat through the task bridge, and records a receipt with specific verification at a work boundary. An idle or archived chat never closes a task, and it creates a chat only when that is explicitly authorized.
brain-work-item.requires: A configured task vault with its task helper and bridge scripts, python3, and the Codex app for creating linked chats.

brand-renderer.what: Render an artifact using the selected visual identity.
brand-renderer.when: A document, deck, workbook, PDF, or page needs branded rendering.
brand-renderer.inputs: The artifact, confirmed brand profile or neutral defaults, and rendering runtime.
brand-renderer.outputs: Rendered files, brand checks, and findings from visual inspection.
brand-renderer.example: Render this report using the confirmed project brand and inspect the exported pages.
brand-renderer.expect: It resolves the selected brand profile (or the neutral policy), proves its runtime with a preflight, then runs parity, visual, prose and brand gates on the rendered artifact. A selected profile that is missing or invalid is an error, and a release needs a written disposition for every warning.

build-interactive-explorer.what: Build an interactive explorer website from source material, with paths, clickable stages, expandable detail and optional roadmaps.
build-interactive-explorer.when: Source material needs a clickable explanation such as a solution explorer, research hub, process guide or journey view.
build-interactive-explorer.inputs: The topic, its sources, and the intended audience and destination.
build-interactive-explorer.outputs: A static explorer site generated from validated content JSON.
build-interactive-explorer.example: Turn these discovery notes into an interactive explorer with seller and enterprise paths and a delivery roadmap.
build-interactive-explorer.expect: It determines the subject from your request and sources, picks one to three paths with ordered stages, and generates a static site from the bundled shell with a content file it validates. It leaves unsupported sections out, does not invent roles, quotes or metrics, and keeps any hosted result private unless you approve otherwise.
build-interactive-explorer.requires: Python 3 for the generator, Node for the JavaScript syntax check, and a new or empty output directory.

business-case.what: Write the business case a funding approver reads, including the case against and the cost of waiting.
business-case.when: An approver needs to decide whether to fund an initiative.
business-case.inputs: A validated evidence ledger, the quote for engagement costs, sourced client value figures and the dated events that drive timing.
business-case.outputs: A gated business case with sourced figures, shown cost-of-delay arithmetic, sourced risks and a bounded ask, or a readiness gap memo when evidence is insufficient.
business-case.example: Build the business case for this initiative from the quote, the discovery findings and the renewal date.
business-case.expect: It builds an evidence ledger first and stops with a readiness gap memo if a load-bearing area is insufficient. The draft must include a case against, shown arithmetic and source tokens on every figure, and a structural gate checks these before release.
business-case.requires: Needs the evidence-core skill, a quote or user-supplied pricing source for cost figures, and python3 to run the case gate.

call-prep.what: Prepare a pursuit or an upcoming sales conversation.
call-prep.when: A pursuit brief, call objective, agenda, or stakeholder plan is needed.
call-prep.inputs: Account evidence, attendees, pursuit context, and the upcoming decision.
call-prep.outputs: A pursuit or call brief with ranked questions and recommended next steps.
call-prep.example: Prepare a call brief for this account with an objective, agenda, and ranked questions.
call-prep.expect: It works in one of two modes: it maintains a Pursuit Brief for the opportunity or prepares one upcoming call from the calendar invite and attendee list. Every claim carries a source, inferences are labeled, figures are reconciled before use, and gaps are reported in chat rather than in the document.
call-prep.requires: Needs the pursuit sources or client profile, the invite or attendee list for a call, and python3 to run the brief checks.

career-application.what: Prepare the user’s application and interview work for a selected role.
career-application.when: Assessing a posting, tailoring materials, or preparing an interview.
career-application.inputs: The current posting, the user’s career sources, and the role work record.
career-application.outputs: Role assessment, tailored materials, interview preparation, or authorized form work.
career-application.example: Assess this posting against my current career direction and prepare the selected application materials.
career-application.reuseNote: Use the caller’s explicitly supplied or authorized sources, configuration, profile and destination. No personal identity or standing permissions transfer with the workflow.
career-application.expect: It reads the candidate's operating context and the live posting first, then runs one role in the mode you name (assess, find, tailor, interview, fill, status or continue). It fills form fields but pauses for salary, work authorization, attestations, CAPTCHA and the final submit, and it marks a role submitted only with a confirmation receipt.
career-application.requires: The candidate's career evidence records (operating context, role work record, base resume), the live posting, and python3 for the readiness checker.

career-materials-and-outreach.what: Draft supporting application materials in the user’s voice.
career-materials-and-outreach.when: A cover letter, form answer, outreach draft, or LinkedIn section is needed.
career-materials-and-outreach.inputs: The role record, current career evidence, and the requested audience.
career-materials-and-outreach.outputs: Complete drafts tied to the role and the user’s supported experience.
career-materials-and-outreach.example: Draft a cover letter for this role from my current role work record.
career-materials-and-outreach.reuseNote: Use the caller’s explicitly supplied or authorized sources, configuration, profile and destination. No personal identity or standing permissions transfer with the workflow.
career-materials-and-outreach.expect: It starts from a role work record with a completed translation table and the tailored resume, then drafts the letter, form answers, outreach, LinkedIn sections or reference packets. Everything is a draft, it pauses without drafting for salary and authorization questions, and sending or publishing needs your separate approval.
career-materials-and-outreach.requires: The candidate's role work record, tailored resume, live posting, professional profile and a confirmed author profile.

career-progression-and-offers.what: Compare roles and offers against the candidate’s chosen career direction.
career-progression-and-offers.when: A role screen, tracker review, negotiation, or offer comparison.
career-progression-and-offers.inputs: Role or offer terms, the user’s criteria, and the current career record.
career-progression-and-offers.outputs: A comparison, open questions, and negotiation drafts for the user’s decision.
career-progression-and-offers.example: Compare these offers against my recorded career gates and list the unresolved terms.
career-progression-and-offers.reuseNote: Use the caller’s explicitly supplied or authorized sources, configuration, profile and destination. No personal identity or standing permissions transfer with the workflow.
career-progression-and-offers.expect: It runs your supplied pay, billability and scope gates and a verified, inferred or unknown progression matrix against a role, the tracker or an offer, and shows each gate result without averaging. It asks for your numbers and weights instead of inventing defaults, drafts negotiation text only after you give a figure, and does not pick between offers.
career-progression-and-offers.requires: The candidate's operating context, tracker, role work record, pay thresholds and the posting or written offer.

case-study-builder.what: Turn the user’s work into a portfolio case study.
case-study-builder.when: A project or engagement needs a case study for the user’s portfolio.
case-study-builder.inputs: Project evidence, the user’s template, and current claims and rights decisions.
case-study-builder.outputs: A working copy and a clean publish copy with unresolved gaps kept in the working record.
case-study-builder.example: Turn this project into a working case study and publish copy using my claims ledger.
case-study-builder.reuseNote: Use the caller’s explicitly supplied or authorized sources, configuration, profile and destination. No personal identity or standing permissions transfer with the workflow.
case-study-builder.expect: It produces two copies each time: a working copy with evidence labels on every figure and a clean publish copy in first person. It brackets missing facts instead of filling them and checks six publish gates, including sanitization and ownership, before anything is called ready.
case-study-builder.requires: The candidate's publication rights ledger, program records and evidence ledger, and a confirmed author profile.

client-brand.what: Apply the confirmed project or client identity.
client-brand.when: An artifact needs a brand profile or existing profile applied.
client-brand.inputs: The project’s confirmed colors, typography, assets, and usage rights.
client-brand.outputs: A selected or updated profile and an artifact checked against it.
client-brand.example: Apply this confirmed brand profile to the document and check the rendered result.
client-brand.expect: It chooses the brand from your explicit choice or the project's brand file, falling back to the neutral Baseline profile, and says which one governs. It marks a new profile as draft until you confirm it and checks the output for mixed identities.

code-simplify.what: Simplify the current code change for reuse, clarity, maintainability and efficiency without changing behavior.
code-simplify.when: A delivery workflow names a simplify pass, or a non-trivial diff needs cleanup before commit.
code-simplify.inputs: The current branch diff or an explicit target, repository conventions and the relevant tests.
code-simplify.outputs: High-confidence refinements with test evidence, plus behavior-changing candidates reported separately instead of applied.
code-simplify.example: Review this diff for duplication and unnecessary complexity while preserving its behavior.
code-simplify.expect: It works on the current branch diff or a target you name, reads the surrounding code and tests, and applies only high-confidence edits for reuse, clarity, maintainability and efficiency. It preserves behavior, stops if the diff base is ambiguous, and reports cleanups that would change behavior as recommendations rather than applying them.
code-simplify.requires: A git repository containing the change, and the project's formatter, static checks and tests.

cross-platform-skill-release.what: Package a skill for Codex and Claude destinations.
cross-platform-skill-release.when: A shared skill needs packaging, replacement, or destination inspection.
cross-platform-skill-release.inputs: The source package, target hosts, and supported installation or upload path.
cross-platform-skill-release.outputs: A portable release package and separately verified destination states.
cross-platform-skill-release.example: Package this reviewed skill for the specified Codex and Claude destinations.
cross-platform-skill-release.expect: It identifies the skill, source and requested destinations, builds the package, and inspects the archive hash and contents before installing or replacing anything. It stops at the destinations you requested, keeps a private replacement private, and reports an upload and a verified invocation as separate states.

cutover-closeout.what: Prepare cutover, hypercare, and delivery closeout.
cutover-closeout.when: An accepted release is approaching go-live or closeout.
cutover-closeout.inputs: Executed scope, release evidence, owners, and the go or no-go decision.
cutover-closeout.outputs: A cutover runbook, acceptance record, hypercare plan, and closeout materials.
cutover-closeout.example: Prepare the cutover runbook and hypercare plan from this accepted release.
cutover-closeout.expect: It builds the cutover runbook, the Go-Live Acceptance tracker, hypercare triage and the closeout record from the executed SOW and the signed readiness pack. It will not plan production cutover without the go decision, will not invent an acceptance deadline the SOW does not support, and leaves acceptance, rollback and closeout approvals to humans.
cutover-closeout.requires: Needs an approved go or no-go decision, the executed SOW, and python3 to run the closeout gate.

ddoc.what: Build a deck for a scope or proposal decision.
ddoc.when: A buyer needs to compare options or confirm one proposal direction.
ddoc.inputs: Scoped options, supporting evidence, commercial inputs, and the decision mode.
ddoc.outputs: A reviewed decision narrative and editable presentation.
ddoc.example: Build a decision deck comparing these two scoped options for the buyer.
ddoc.expect: It pins the mode (decision or confirmation), audience and quote source, builds a manifest, and gates it with a no-render check before any slide-by-slide copy approval. It refuses to render on a preflight failure or an unresolved flag, and on an unattended run it stops before approvals instead of simulating them.
ddoc.requires: Needs a quote identifier with its source data, Node for the gate, pptxgenjs to render the PPTX, and python-pptx to extract an existing deck.

deal-desk.what: Prepare the internal Deal Desk packet that shows a deal's computed margin against the approval policy.
deal-desk.when: A priced quote needs internal commercial approval before proposal or SOW, or a packet's figures need tie-out.
deal-desk.inputs: The quote, the confirmed margin floor and approval ladder, the evidence ledger and the delivery lead's cosign answer.
deal-desk.outputs: A gated packet with recomputed margin, flagged risks, routed asks, an empty decisions log and a figure tie-out against the quote.
deal-desk.example: Prepare the Deal Desk packet for this quote and tie out the SOW draft's figures against it.
deal-desk.expect: It orients on the quote, confirms the margin floor and approval ladder, then builds a readout with margin as the headline and every flag visible. It asks for the delivery cosign rather than inferring it, recomputes margin in a gate, and never adjusts hours or rates to rescue a number.
deal-desk.requires: Needs a priced quote (Q-number) or export, the project's margin floor and approval policy, and python3 to run the gate and tie-out.

deck-builder.what: Build a presentation around the audience’s decision.
deck-builder.when: A pitch, proposal, reading deck, or technical briefing is needed.
deck-builder.inputs: The audience, decision, source evidence, and output requirements.
deck-builder.outputs: An editable deck with reviewed copy, explanatory visuals, and rendered checks.
deck-builder.example: Create a briefing deck that helps this audience decide between the supported options.
deck-builder.expect: It saves a brief, one-sentence thesis, submessages, slide structure and copy as separate records, in that order, before building anything. The thesis must pass a gate before slides are planned, and a QA pass over the finished deck is written up as a polish list.
deck-builder.requires: Needs an engagement folder with a brief (audience and decision), python3 for the HTML build, and a presentation tool for PowerPoint output.

delivery-kickoff.what: Mobilize a signed engagement from the accepted handoff and the signed SOW.
delivery-kickoff.when: The sales-to-delivery handoff is accepted and kickoff is next.
delivery-kickoff.inputs: The accepted handoff brief, the signed SOW, the confirmed delivery model and the shared engagement record.
delivery-kickoff.outputs: A gated draft charter, seeded RAID and decision logs, internal and client kickoff decks, and a Sprint 0 or mobilization plan.
delivery-kickoff.example: Prepare the charter, governance logs and kickoff decks from the signed SOW and the accepted handoff.
delivery-kickoff.expect: It starts from the accepted handoff brief and signed SOW and drafts the charter, RAID and decision logs, kickoff decks and Sprint 0 plan. It stops if no accepted handoff exists, restates SOW scope without renegotiating it, and drafts what humans sign without signing or provisioning anything.
delivery-kickoff.requires: Needs an accepted sales-to-delivery handoff brief, the signed SOW, and python3 to run the charter check.

delivery-status.what: Issue the period's delivery status, steward the RAID and decision logs, and check work against the SOW scope.
delivery-status.when: A weekly status report, a decision or risk to log, or a check of whether a request is in scope.
delivery-status.inputs: The period's transcripts, the RAID and decision logs, the SOW scope baseline, the previous status file and a timesheet or quote for burn.
delivery-status.outputs: A gated status report, append-only log entries with stable IDs, and change-order candidates with an evidence trail.
delivery-status.example: Write this week's status from the transcripts and logs, and flag anything that looks outside the SOW.
delivery-status.expect: It pins the engagement, the exact period and the previous status file, then reads the period's transcripts and updates the RAID and decision logs with stable IDs. It flags scope drift as a change-order candidate with quoted evidence, shows burn only from a named source, and a blocking gate must pass before the report is issued.
delivery-status.requires: Needs the RAID and decision logs from kickoff, the SOW scope baseline, the period's transcripts, and python3 to run the status gate.

delivery-suite.what: Route delivery work to the appropriate stage and owner.
delivery-suite.when: A signed engagement needs coordination across delivery stages.
delivery-suite.inputs: Executed scope, current delivery state, and the requested decision.
delivery-suite.outputs: An updated stage record and the next owning workflow or gate.
delivery-suite.example: Review this engagement’s delivery state and route the next work to its owner.
delivery-suite.expect: It reads the engagement's DELIVERY-STATE.md, runs the planner to find the current stage and the next gate, and hands the work to the skill that owns it by name. It builds no artifacts itself, never marks a gate passed without its signed record, and does not touch pre-signature work.
delivery-suite.requires: Needs the engagement's DELIVERY-STATE.md (or the hard evidence to write one) and python3 to run the planner.

discovery-brief.what: Maintain the findings and open questions for a pursuit.
discovery-brief.when: Preparing discovery or incorporating a completed call.
discovery-brief.inputs: The pursuit record, source notes, and scope or pricing questions.
discovery-brief.outputs: A sourced discovery ledger and ranked questions that unblock the pursuit.
discovery-brief.example: Update the pursuit ledger from this call and rank the unanswered scope questions.
discovery-brief.expect: It builds a two-column ledger of supported facts and ranked open questions tied to the scope each one unblocks, before and after a discovery session. A transcript is ingested to close questions only with evidence, a priced unresolved item fails the brief, and it never creates hours, rates or fees.
discovery-brief.requires: Needs the pursuit's sources (RFP, CRM record, transcripts, client documents) and python3 to run the ledger check.

discovery-synthesis.what: Turn discovery calls and interview notes into sourced research findings.
discovery-synthesis.when: Supplied meeting content needs synthesis into what was learned.
discovery-synthesis.inputs: Transcripts or notes, the attendees on each side and the research purpose.
discovery-synthesis.outputs: A TL;DR, job statements, pain points with severity, exact quotes, speaker insights, open questions and named gaps.
discovery-synthesis.example: Synthesize these three discovery calls into findings, pain points and exact quotes with speakers.
discovery-synthesis.expect: It first confirms the client, meeting type and who attended, then reads the whole transcript or notes and separates client voices from the consulting team's. It quotes only words present in the source, rates severity from the source wording, and will not call the result final until the writing review and quality gate have passed.
discovery-synthesis.requires: Needs the call content itself (pasted notes, a text, Word or PDF file, or a Granola transcript through its connector) and a confirmed client and project context; audio files are not accepted.

dx-devops-promote.what: Prepare and perform an authorized DevOps Center promotion.
dx-devops-promote.when: Work items or a pipeline stage need promotion.
dx-devops-promote.inputs: The configured integration, target stage, work items, and authorization.
dx-devops-promote.outputs: Capability and dependency checks, promotion results, and unresolved conflicts.
dx-devops-promote.example: Check whether these work items are ready for promotion to the specified stage.
dx-devops-promote.expect: It runs a local capability check first, then verifies the confirmed target org and always runs promotion validation before anything is changed. It stops at a failed check, a missing org or a missing plugin capability instead of guessing, and does not claim a deployment succeeded from a started command.

dx-devops-work-item-manage.what: Manage DevOps Center work items and review requests.
dx-devops-work-item-manage.when: Creating, updating, committing, or reviewing a work item.
dx-devops-work-item-manage.inputs: The configured integration, selected work item, and requested operation.
dx-devops-work-item-manage.outputs: The verified work-item change, commit, or review request.
dx-devops-work-item-manage.example: Inspect this DevOps Center work item and prepare the requested field update.
dx-devops-work-item-manage.expect: It asks for the confirmed target org, the operation (list, create, update, commit or open a pull request) and the project or work item, then checks the DevOps Center plugin before changing anything. It stops if the plugin or the org login is missing and confirms a status change from the returned result.

evidence-core.what: Track source records and the claims an artifact can support.
evidence-core.when: A material client artifact needs evidence review.
evidence-core.inputs: The project sources, revisions, authority rules, and proposed claims.
evidence-core.outputs: A source register, atomic claims, conflicts, and an evidence sufficiency decision.
evidence-core.example: Build a claim ledger for this report using these versioned sources.
evidence-core.expect: It builds a ledger of sources and atomic claims first, with an authority score, status and owner for anything unresolved, and the document comes after. If a load-bearing area has too little evidence it writes a short readiness-gap memo and stops instead of drafting the full artifact.
evidence-core.requires: Needs source files or exports for the engagement, a Knowledge Hub location for the evidence records, and Python 3 to run the ledger validator.

execution-truth.what: Verify what changed and where the result exists.
execution-truth.when: Work changes files, repositories, deployments, installations, or cloud records.
execution-truth.inputs: The intended result, affected destination, and available verification access.
execution-truth.outputs: A precise completion state with evidence and the remaining action.
execution-truth.example: Verify which parts of this release are local, merged, published, and installed.
execution-truth.expect: It identifies the requested outcome, the authoritative source and the finish line before work starts, then checks the destination system when the work ends. It will not report a local draft, commit or API response as a later state such as merged or live, and ends with what changed, what was verified, what is unchanged and the next action.

fortunes-weave.what: Answer questions and maintain the user’s Fortune’s Weave planner.
fortunes-weave.when: A question concerns the user’s current route, roster, or planner.
fortunes-weave.inputs: Her current project router, route sources, roster, and live planner state.
fortunes-weave.outputs: A sourced answer or an authorized, verified planner update.
fortunes-weave.example: Check my current route and roster before recommending the next planner update.
fortunes-weave.reuseNote: Use the caller’s explicitly supplied or authorized sources, configuration, profile and destination. No personal identity or standing permissions transfer with the workflow.
fortunes-weave.expect: It reads the live roster and planner state before recommending a team or changing a build, and pulls only the researched section it needs. It will not state niche game mechanics from memory or treat a suggested team as a confirmed roster, and it asks for a roster export if it cannot reach the planner.
fortunes-weave.requires: Needs the planner project location and its current roster, either readable through an available tool or supplied as an export.

github-repository-work.what: Work with the user’s GitHub repositories.
github-repository-work.when: A repository needs inspection, a commit, a PR, or release work.
github-repository-work.inputs: The explicitly identified repository, intended account and authorized change.
github-repository-work.outputs: Verified repository changes and separate PR, merge, or deployment state.
github-repository-work.example: Review this specified repository change and prepare a pull request.
github-repository-work.reuseNote: Use the caller’s explicitly supplied or authorized sources, configuration, profile and destination. No personal identity or standing permissions transfer with the workflow.
github-repository-work.expect: It inspects the remote, branch and working tree, then checks that the GitHub CLI can reach the named host, owner and repository before acting. It reads back the remote commit or pull request after a push, and it does not bypass protected branches, reviews or environment approvals or ask for a token.
github-repository-work.requires: Needs Git and the GitHub CLI (gh) installed and logged in to the target host with access to the repository.

independent-product.what: Develop the user’s independent work from supplied historical projects.
independent-product.when: An employer-era artifact is being translated into an independent product or offer.
independent-product.inputs: Authorized historical sources, a project brief, and claims and rights decisions.
independent-product.outputs: A usable independent artifact or backlog with source and publication questions resolved where possible.
independent-product.example: Translate these authorized historical materials into an independent offering brief.
independent-product.reuseNote: Use the caller’s explicitly supplied or authorized sources, configuration, profile and destination. No personal identity or standing permissions transfer with the workflow.
independent-product.expect: It first confirms the user's authority and the reuse scope from the task, then drafts a short migration map of the useful mechanism, its original dependencies and the independent form. It rebuilds examples with synthetic data, removes client details before anything leaves the private workspace, and treats publication as a separate decision.
independent-product.requires: Needs the historical project material and a user-selected home for the independent product.

information-architecture.what: Organize navigation, content labels, and site structure.
information-architecture.when: A website or product needs better findability.
information-architecture.inputs: The audience, content inventory, tasks, and current navigation.
information-architecture.outputs: A sitemap, taxonomy, navigation proposal, or structural review.
information-architecture.example: Reorganize this site’s navigation around the tasks visitors need to complete.
information-architecture.expect: It reads the current content inventory and navigation before proposing anything, then gives a sitemap or structure with reasons tied to the audience's tasks. It keeps existing URLs unless a change is authorized, and it labels the result provisional because only real card sorts or tree tests count as validation.

interactive-proposal.what: Build a page for exploring scope options.
interactive-proposal.when: A priced proposal or an unpriced scope explorer is needed.
interactive-proposal.inputs: Versioned scope, options, assumptions, and confirmed prices when applicable.
interactive-proposal.outputs: An interactive HTML page with selectable options and reconciled figures.
interactive-proposal.example: Create an interactive comparison of these scope options using the confirmed quote figures.
interactive-proposal.expect: It announces whether it is in Proposal mode (a priced quote exists) or Explorer mode (no quote, so no currency anywhere) and builds one self-contained HTML page. A source mismatch or unsupported fee blocks the build, and the page is not deliverable until parity, visual and prose checks each have a written result.
interactive-proposal.requires: Needs a quote export or source documents, and Python 3 for the builder; browser checks also need Node.js, Playwright and Chromium.

journey-mapping.what: Map a customer or role’s experience and the service underneath.
journey-mapping.when: A journey map, service blueprint, or opportunity map is needed.
journey-mapping.inputs: Touchpoints, research, goals, friction, roles, and system evidence.
journey-mapping.outputs: A journey or blueprint with sourced findings and labeled hypotheses.
journey-mapping.example: Map this customer journey from research through the service and systems underneath.
journey-mapping.expect: It confirms the actor, the starting and ending events and the decision first, then produces a journey map, a service blueprint and an opportunity map that share one set of phases. Every claim is sourced or labeled as a hypothesis, and a release check it cannot run is reported as missing instead of passed.
journey-mapping.requires: Needs a named actor and journey plus sources such as transcripts, tickets, analytics or system records; without interviews it can only draft the human layers as labeled hypotheses.

jtbd-framing.what: Frame the job a person is trying to accomplish and test whether the framing changes a decision.
jtbd-framing.when: Job statements, struggling moments, hire and fire criteria, or an audit of existing JTBD work are needed.
jtbd-framing.inputs: Research about recent struggling moments and switch decisions, or a request for hypotheses with interview prompts when none exists.
jtbd-framing.outputs: Job framing with evidence references, decision implications, remaining research questions and an audit against twelve checks.
jtbd-framing.example: Extract the struggling moments and hire criteria from these interviews before drafting job statements.
jtbd-framing.expect: It works from struggling moments and hire and fire criteria in the research you supply, and writes job statements only where the source shows the outcome. With no research it produces hypotheses marked as such plus interview prompts, and it will say when the framing only restates a feature list.
jtbd-framing.requires: Needs interview or switch-decision research to state factual jobs; without it the output is limited to labeled hypotheses and interview prompts.

knowledge-hub.what: Retrieve and maintain a project’s durable knowledge.
knowledge-hub.when: Work needs current client, pursuit, engagement, or evidence records.
knowledge-hub.inputs: The confirmed project identity, permitted storage, and relevant sources.
knowledge-hub.outputs: Retrieved context or verified workspace and record updates.
knowledge-hub.example: Find the current discovery and decision records for this opportunity in the permitted store.
knowledge-hub.expect: It confirms the client and the opportunity or engagement first and stops if identity is ambiguous, then reads the front door and only the records the task needs. Writes go to the declared primary store only, with a hash check, and it reports one of five persistence states, so a returned patch is never described as an update.
knowledge-hub.requires: Needs a hub folder, a Google Drive hub or supplied files, and Python 3 to run the record and workspace scripts.

author-writing-style.what: Apply an explicitly selected author’s confirmed writing profile.
author-writing-style.when: The task names an author and provides or authorizes their profile.
author-writing-style.inputs: The draft, sources, intended author and confirmed profile.
author-writing-style.outputs: Complete prose preserving supported claims and confirmed author preferences.
author-writing-style.example: Rewrite this About draft in my voice while preserving its supported claims.
author-writing-style.reuseNote: Use the caller’s explicitly supplied or authorized sources, configuration, profile and destination. No personal identity or standing permissions transfer with the workflow.
author-writing-style.expect: It uses a writing profile only when one for the named author is supplied or authorized for the task, and reads the profile's ownership and revocation state first. With no profile it falls back to plain drafting, and it will not claim a profile was loaded or a scan was run when it was not.
author-writing-style.requires: A confirmed author writing profile supplied in the task or held in an authorized private profile store.

org-preflight.what: Verify the Salesforce organization before a write.
org-preflight.when: A Salesforce record change, upload, or deployment is about to occur.
org-preflight.inputs: The intended org ID, sandbox status, connection, and requested action.
org-preflight.outputs: A current identity check and a proceed or stop decision.
org-preflight.example: Verify the intended Salesforce org ID and sandbox status before this record update.
org-preflight.expect: It queries the Organization record on the named connection and compares the org ID and sandbox flag with the intended target. It refuses a missing, unknown, mismatched or malformed identity, requires an explicit flag for production, and a pass does not authorize the deployment.

personal-writing-style-runtime.what: Apply one person’s confirmed writing profile.
personal-writing-style-runtime.when: The intended author has an approved private style profile.
personal-writing-style-runtime.inputs: That author’s profile, its scope, and a configured installation adapter.
personal-writing-style-runtime.outputs: Writing reviewed against the selected author’s profile.
personal-writing-style-runtime.example: Apply the confirmed author profile to this draft within its stated scope.
personal-writing-style-runtime.expect: It first decides who the author is, plus the surface, audience and purpose, and applies a confirmed profile only when the profiled person is the author. It falls back to plain drafting when the profile has no confirmed entry for that case, and never applies it to quotations or organizational voice.

playbook-builder.what: Define and maintain a productized service offering.
playbook-builder.when: An offering needs definition, comparison, or catalog maintenance.
playbook-builder.inputs: The buyer, problem, proposed service, scope, and current catalog.
playbook-builder.outputs: A structured offering with value, deliverables, boundaries, and catalog decisions.
playbook-builder.example: Define the buyer, value, deliverables, and boundaries for this service offering.
playbook-builder.expect: It works out which job you want (define, audit, deduplicate, add or replace, maintain), then answers the seven Clarity questions before rendering anything in the house format. It will not invent prices, durations or figures, lists open choices as decisions to lock, and checks that untouched catalog entries stayed byte-identical.
playbook-builder.requires: Needs the existing catalog file when editing one, and Python 3 for the corpus verifier.

playbook-fit-router.what: Match a prospect’s needs to an offering.
playbook-fit-router.when: Discovery needs to become an offering-fit decision.
playbook-fit-router.inputs: The current offering catalog and supported prospect findings.
playbook-fit-router.outputs: Ranked fit, evidence behind the score, disqualifiers, and open questions.
playbook-fit-router.example: Compare this prospect’s discovery findings with our current offering catalog.
playbook-fit-router.expect: It reads the discovery material and scores signals against each playbook's qualifier, citing the source of every point. It returns a ranked top three with the unanswered gates as the next call's agenda, does not price or lock a tier, and treats a run without the approved qualifier schema as diagnostic only.

playbook-onepager.what: Render an offering into sales handouts.
playbook-onepager.when: A defined offering needs internal enablement or an external handout.
playbook-onepager.inputs: Structured offering content and the selected brand profile.
playbook-onepager.outputs: A two-page internal brief and one-page external PDF, checked after rendering.
playbook-onepager.example: Render this defined offering as an internal brief and an external handout.
playbook-onepager.expect: It renders one playbook into a two-page internal brief and a one-page external PDF from structured Markdown or a JSON spec, using the confirmed brand profile or the neutral one. It adds no claims to fill a slot, fails on missing content, overflow or a wrong page count, and keeps failed attempts instead of overwriting them.
playbook-onepager.requires: Needs Python 3 with Jinja2 and pypdf, plus Node.js, Playwright and Chromium installed locally through the setup steps in the instructions.

playbook-suite.what: Plan and track the artifacts for an offering.
playbook-suite.when: An offering needs a complete artifact package or readiness review.
playbook-suite.inputs: The offering definition, manifest, existing artifacts, and commercial policy.
playbook-suite.outputs: An artifact plan, owning workflows, and remaining readiness checks.
playbook-suite.example: Review this offering’s artifact manifest and identify what remains before release.
playbook-suite.expect: It runs a planner against the playbook's manifest and reports the ordered build plan with every finding, then works one ready artifact at a time. Nothing is marked complete without three written gate results, and because the approved specification is supplied by the caller its output says release readiness is unverified.

pm-spec-writing.when: A feature needs a PRD, development brief, or acceptance criteria.
pm-spec-writing.inputs: The problem, users, evidence, constraints, and requested scope.
pm-spec-writing.outputs: A specification with behavior, requirements, and testable acceptance criteria.
pm-spec-writing.example: Write a feature specification with user behavior, requirements, and acceptance criteria.
pm-spec-writing.expect: It reads the brief, sources and existing decisions first, then drafts a spec at the depth the change needs with observable acceptance criteria. It asks only about a decision that blocks useful work, drafts the supported parts meanwhile, and will not invent a baseline, estimate, date or owner.

prioritization.what: Rank candidates with a named framework and check the evidence behind each score.
prioritization.when: A team must choose between problems, outcomes, roadmap candidates or backlog items.
prioritization.inputs: Candidates with their scoring inputs and the source for each input.
prioritization.outputs: A ranked proposal with each item's formula, flagged unsourced inputs and ties, and the decision owner named.
prioritization.example: RICE-score these eight roadmap candidates and flag any score that rests on a guess.
prioritization.expect: It names what is being ranked and picks one framework with a stated reason, then collects each score input with a source and runs a scoring script. The output is a ranked proposal with formulas, flags and a named decision owner, and the flags are carried forward, not cleared by raising a number.
prioritization.requires: Needs a candidate list with sourced inputs for the chosen framework and Python 3 for the scoring script.

process.what: Document a process or identify improvements.
process.when: An SOP, ownership map, or process optimization is needed.
process.inputs: The current steps, roles, exceptions, constraints, and available measures.
process.outputs: An SOP or improvement analysis covering time, cost, quality, and ownership.
process.example: Document this approval process as an SOP with owners, exceptions, and measures.
process.expect: It picks Document mode (an SOP with a RACI) or Optimize mode from your request, and asks targeted questions when the description is thin. It writes not captured or open: for missing owners, durations and figures, and will not invent an impact estimate.

product-development-pathway.what: Develop a product from its current evidence and release state.
product-development-pathway.when: Starting or resuming a product at a requested stage.
product-development-pathway.inputs: The product brief, current sources, decisions, and readiness evidence.
product-development-pathway.outputs: An updated product record and the next supported development action.
product-development-pathway.example: Resume this product at its current stage using the recorded readiness evidence.
product-development-pathway.expect: It enters at the stage you request, reuses the existing product home and decisions, and keeps source review, product decision and implementation evidence as separate states. It records readiness gates for the stage, names the next action with its required authorization, and never reports proposed or local work as released or live.
product-development-pathway.requires: Needs an existing product home or an authorized place to create one, plus the supplied source material for the stage.

prose-pass.what: Run the writing diagnostics and figure checks that writing-integrity uses.
prose-pass.when: Writing-integrity needs a pattern scan, a figure tie-out or a review receipt.
prose-pass.inputs: The saved text, the source version for figure comparison and the house configuration.
prose-pass.outputs: Pattern findings, figure comparisons and validated review receipts; it does not rewrite text.
prose-pass.example: Check this saved draft for recurring writing patterns and confirm no figure changed from the source.
prose-pass.expect: It is an internal checker used by the writing review, not an editor, and it reports detectable patterns in a saved file by exit code without rewriting anything. It can reconcile figures between a source and a rewrite and emit a review receipt, but a clean scan does not show the prose was read.
prose-pass.requires: Needs Python 3 and a saved file to check.

quality-gate.what: Review a finished artifact against the request and sources.
quality-gate.when: A material deliverable is approaching release.
quality-gate.inputs: The artifact, controlling sources, output requirements, and actual checks.
quality-gate.outputs: A release decision with supported findings and required repairs.
quality-gate.example: Review this deliverable against its sources, requested outcome, and rendered form.
quality-gate.expect: It opens the finished artifact and its sources, then records each required check as pass, fail, blocked or not applicable with cited evidence. A missing prose receipt, brand report or source for a claim blocks release, and it returns a remediation list instead of marking anything complete.
quality-gate.requires: Needs the finished artifact and its evidence record, and Python 3 to run the quality record validator.

requirements-capture.what: Turn source material into a structured requirements backlog through a guided conversation.
requirements-capture.when: Requirements, user stories or a SOW-to-backlog workbook are needed.
requirements-capture.inputs: The brief, SOW, transcripts or product sources, and confirmation of the proposed hierarchy.
requirements-capture.outputs: A two-tab Excel workbook of epics, capabilities, business needs, stories, Gherkin acceptance criteria and MoSCoW priorities.
requirements-capture.example: Turn this SOW into a requirements workbook with stories and testable acceptance criteria.
requirements-capture.expect: It starts with a conversation, not a file: it reads your source material, proposes the epic hierarchy and asks you to confirm it before generating anything. It then builds a two-tab Excel workbook with Gherkin acceptance criteria and MoSCoW priorities, defaults unclear priority to Must Have with flagged assumptions, and keeps versioned copies as you revise.
requirements-capture.requires: Needs source material (deck, PRD, brief or transcript, or a Salesforce SOW in BA mode) and a spreadsheet skill with a recalculation script available to build the workbook.

resume-numbers-and-keywords.what: Apply the user’s resume methods for figures and ATS wording.
resume-numbers-and-keywords.when: Her tailored resume needs quantified bullets or keyword placement.
resume-numbers-and-keywords.inputs: Current career evidence, the posting, and the draft resume.
resume-numbers-and-keywords.outputs: Revised bullets and layout that preserve the user’s stated scope and evidence.
resume-numbers-and-keywords.example: Review my resume bullets against this posting and the current source figures.
resume-numbers-and-keywords.reuseNote: Use the caller’s explicitly supplied or authorized sources, configuration, profile and destination. No personal identity or standing permissions transfer with the workflow.
resume-numbers-and-keywords.expect: It loads the role's work record, master resume, live posting and claim records first, and stops if the narrative translation table is empty. Figures are stated or estimated with the arithmetic recorded, keywords go in only where the evidence supports them, and a bullet never gets an ownership claim the sources do not make.
resume-numbers-and-keywords.requires: Needs the candidate's confirmed career records (operating context, role work record, master resume and evidence ledger) and the live posting or its saved snapshot.

roadmap-artifacts.what: Build roadmaps from one fixed set of branded, interactive components.
roadmap-artifacts.when: A roadmap, timeline, launch plan or delivery plan is needed as a page or inside another page.
roadmap-artifacts.inputs: The work to plan, the governing brand profile, and connected sources when the data lives in a tool.
roadmap-artifacts.outputs: A validated plan JSON rendered as a branded page, an embeddable element or a single-file estate page.
roadmap-artifacts.example: Build a now, next, later roadmap for these initiatives in our confirmed brand.
roadmap-artifacts.expect: It picks a template from its catalog, resolves the brand profile and states it, then writes a plan JSON and builds the roadmap with a script that validates the plan and reports any neutral substitutions and contrast warnings. It uses only confirmed brand values, never ships guessed live-data paths, and never writes back to a source tool.
roadmap-artifacts.requires: Python 3 to run the build script, and a confirmed brand profile if the roadmap should carry one.

rom.what: Estimate a rough effort or cost range.
rom.when: A pursuit needs an early estimate and its basis.
rom.inputs: Supplied scope, comparables, assumptions, and rates when available.
rom.outputs: A sourced estimate range with calculations and reopening conditions.
rom.example: Estimate a rough effort range from these scope items and comparable projects.
rom.expect: It pins the audience, runs the evidence review, then builds a cost and effort range with a basis-of-estimate table where each figure carries its source and confidence. Unconfirmed dimensions show as flagged assumptions, a quote that fails to reconcile is reported with its discrepancy rather than smoothed, and the range is never presented as a quote.
rom.requires: A supplied scope plus a rate card, comparables or an existing quote, and Python 3 for the reconciliation gate.

s2d-handoff.what: Prepare the handoff from sales to delivery.
s2d-handoff.when: A signed engagement needs a receiving delivery owner.
s2d-handoff.inputs: The executed agreement, quote, deal record, and receiving team.
s2d-handoff.outputs: A handoff package with ownership, assumptions, and tracked acceptance.
s2d-handoff.example: Prepare the sales-to-delivery handoff from the executed agreement and deal record.
s2d-handoff.expect: It confirms the deal is signed, gathers facts from the executed SOW, quote and deal record, and builds a 12-section handoff manifest that a script gate checks. Every section is filled or carries a named gap with an owner, and it stops with a gap memo if required evidence is insufficient; it never records an acceptance nobody gave.
s2d-handoff.requires: An executed SOW and its quote for a signed deal, plus Python 3 to run the manifest gate.

sales-journey-critique.what: Review a sales journey, demo, or proposed workflow.
sales-journey-critique.when: A journey needs specific corrections to steps, systems, or measures.
sales-journey-critique.inputs: The journey or demo, customer task, current workflow, and proposed change.
sales-journey-critique.outputs: A critique tracing the task and recommending supported corrections.
sales-journey-critique.example: Trace this demo against the customer’s task and recommend specific workflow corrections.
sales-journey-critique.expect: It reads the artifact and its source evidence first, then checks five things: customer flow, current versus future state, systems, click paths and measures. It returns a prioritized critique with the first repair to make, and it stops before any purchase, submission, message or live record change unless you authorize it.

sales-process-mapping.what: Map a sales process from its source files.
sales-process-mapping.when: Ownership, triggers, handoffs, or systems of record need clarification.
sales-process-mapping.inputs: Discovery files, workbooks, CRM or Jira exports, and operating notes.
sales-process-mapping.outputs: A process explanation, diagram, ownership tables, and unresolved questions.
sales-process-mapping.example: Map the sales process from these files. Identify owners, triggers, handoffs, systems of record, and unresolved questions.
sales-process-mapping.expect: It inventories your files and exports, reads them completely, and maps each process from trigger to completion with owners, handoffs, record grain and system of record, plus territory and opportunity ownership when relevant. Gaps stay as open questions with locators rather than guessed rules, and it will not change CRM records, territories or Jira issues.

scope-reference.what: Compare scope options in a static document.
scope-reference.when: A printable scope summary or option matrix is needed.
scope-reference.inputs: One versioned quote or export with scope, hours, staffing, price, and timeline.
scope-reference.outputs: A reconciled scope summary or side-by-side option comparison.
scope-reference.example: Create a printable comparison of these options from one confirmed quote revision.
scope-reference.expect: It asks for the client, quote IDs and order, then needs either a quote connector or a dated quote export. It reconciles every scope item, hour value, status and staffing-snapshot price with a validator before building a self-contained HTML page, and it stops the build if no real scope records are supplied.
scope-reference.requires: A current quote connection or a dated quote export, and Python 3 for the validator and builder.

scoping-agent.what: Develop scope, effort, staffing, and timeline estimates.
scoping-agent.when: A project needs a rough range or a confirmed quote revision.
scoping-agent.inputs: The brief, scope model, comparables, rate card, and relevant constraints.
scoping-agent.outputs: Scope items and estimates with shown calculations. Unknown effort remains visible as unestimated. Staffing and schedule bounds follow the supplied capacity and dependencies.
scoping-agent.example: Estimate effort, staffing, and timing for this scope using the supplied rate card.
scoping-agent.expect: It reads your brief first, then builds scope items with sources and acceptance conditions and, when asked, a low, expected and high effort range from a local calculator. Work with no effort basis stays unestimated, totals are marked incomplete, and it changes a quote record only inside an authorized request.
scoping-agent.requires: Python 3 for the local estimate calculator, plus a rate card or confirmed quote if you want a cost figure.

session-handoff.what: Prepare another session to resume the same work.
session-handoff.when: The current session is ending or needs a handoff.
session-handoff.inputs: The session’s decisions, files, running state, and completed checks.
session-handoff.outputs: A handoff with the current state, verification, open questions, and exact next action.
session-handoff.example: Prepare a handoff with the current files, decisions, verification, and exact next action.
session-handoff.expect: It stamps the time, directory and git state once, then writes a fixed-template handoff from what happened in the session, with absolute paths and 'none' for empty sections. It prints the handoff in chat and saves a file only where a handoffs directory already exists, and it does not audit the filesystem or update memory.

sf-delivery-standards.what: Install, audit or repair a Salesforce repository's delivery standards.
sf-delivery-standards.when: A project needs its hooks, instruction contract, tracker or trunk settings set up, checked or fixed.
sf-delivery-standards.inputs: The repository, its delivery mode, tracker, host and ownership mode, and authenticated prerequisites.
sf-delivery-standards.outputs: Installed or repaired hooks and contract blocks, recorded configuration, and an audit result for each piece.
sf-delivery-standards.example: Audit this Salesforce repository's delivery hooks and project instructions, and fix what is no longer armed.
sf-delivery-standards.expect: It runs a prerequisites check first, asks only for settings it cannot detect (tracker, trunk branch, platform), then installs hooks and a managed instruction block, audits what it installed and prints a client-conversation checklist. It never accepts a pasted credential, directing you to the browser login commands instead, and the audit is read-only unless you add --fix.

sf-deploy-engine.what: Operate an existing sf-deploy-engine Salesforce pipeline.
sf-deploy-engine.when: A pipeline environment needs status, promotion, a release, rollback, revalidation or freeze recovery.
sf-deploy-engine.inputs: The repository's pipeline.yml, a privately stored engine token and the authorized tickets or SHAs.
sf-deploy-engine.outputs: Engine status and the verified result of the requested operation.
sf-deploy-engine.example: Check the engine's status and release GH-397 from preprod to main.
sf-deploy-engine.expect: It works from the repo's pipeline.yml and reports status, promotes, cuts releases, rolls back by ticket or SHA, or runs a read-only doctor check. It refuses to run a manual sf deploy against a pipeline environment's org, and it states that its guards stop an agent in this session, not a person deploying from a terminal.

sf-enterprise-patterns.what: Apply the estate Salesforce architecture and check code against it.
sf-enterprise-patterns.when: Apex, trigger or LWC work in a project that uses service, selector and unit-of-work conventions.
sf-enterprise-patterns.inputs: The codebase, its architecture decisions and the requested feature or review.
sf-enterprise-patterns.outputs: Code or a review aligned to the layers, with architecture checker findings reported separately from judgment findings.
sf-enterprise-patterns.example: Review this Apex change against the project's service, selector and unit-of-work patterns.
sf-enterprise-patterns.expect: It reads your project's architecture decisions first, then structures Apex and LWC into trigger, service, selector, unit-of-work and controller layers and runs arch_check.py. The checker exits 1 on a blocking violation, suppressions need a stated reason, and if adoption is undecided it reports findings and leaves enforcement uninstalled.

sf-headless-screenshot.what: Capture Salesforce UI evidence and run clickpath checks.
sf-headless-screenshot.when: An authorized UI path needs screenshots or assertions.
sf-headless-screenshot.inputs: The org connection, supported screenshot runtime, and target path.
sf-headless-screenshot.outputs: Screenshots, clickpath results, and observed UI issues.
sf-headless-screenshot.example: Capture this Salesforce clickpath and check its stated acceptance conditions.
sf-headless-screenshot.expect: It needs a confirmed org alias and a page or record, and checks that the selected sfqa tool exists before running anything. It captures screenshots or runs clickpath assertions and reports a screenshot as not ready if a load stage timed out; if no supported tool or browser is available, it reports the check as pending rather than improvising.

sf-solo-devops.what: Deliver a change to a single-org Salesforce project.
sf-solo-devops.when: An authorized Salesforce change needs the project delivery workflow.
sf-solo-devops.inputs: The issue, repository, target org, configuration, and requested change.
sf-solo-devops.outputs: The change with separate validation, review, deployment, and acceptance evidence.
sf-solo-devops.example: Prepare this authorized Salesforce change using the project’s isolated delivery workflow.
sf-solo-devops.expect: It requires a GitHub issue first, then works in an isolated worktree with local checks, a per-commit dry run against a confirmed org, a squash merge and a deploy from main. With no org it stops at 'prepared locally' and never records a validation or deployment as done, and it counts the task finished only when the ticket is closed and the worktree removed.

skill-creation-walkthrough.what: Create or repair a workflow for the Skills Estate.
skill-creation-walkthrough.when: An estate addition, collision review or behavioral repair.
skill-creation-walkthrough.inputs: The recurring task, example requests, source methods, and expected outputs.
skill-creation-walkthrough.outputs: The preserved workflow, governed intake, metadata, required resources and validation evidence.
skill-creation-walkthrough.example: Create a focused skill from this repeated workflow and these example requests.
skill-creation-walkthrough.expect: It first checks the closest existing skills and asks whether the task belongs in a skill at all, then records a collision decision and intake before scaffolding a draft outside the installed set. It tests a positive, an alternate and a nearby negative request, and creating a draft never installs it.
skill-creation-walkthrough.requires: A Skills Estate checkout and Python 3 for the scaffolder and checks.

skill-estate-sync.what: Maintain a Skills Estate checkout by authoring, validating, packaging and releasing workflows.
skill-estate-sync.when: A workflow needs creating or repair, packages need building, a reviewed release needs installing, or another host needs an update.
skill-estate-sync.inputs: The canonical estate checkout, the reviewed source hash for installation and the target host.
skill-estate-sync.outputs: Validation and build results, packages, installation receipts and publication records for the requested operation.
skill-estate-sync.example: Validate the current estate and build candidate packages without installing them.
skill-estate-sync.expect: It works only on the confirmed estate checkout and runs the single operation you ask for, such as validate, build, bundle, status or install. Install needs the exact reviewed source hash, refuses to overwrite a divergent installation, and a successful build is reported as packaging only, not proof the skill works.

solution-brief.what: Decide whether a proposed client solution can be delivered and make its delivery logic inspectable.
solution-brief.when: A solution needs deal approval, a build reference for developers or a field guide for a scoping call.
solution-brief.inputs: A validated evidence ledger and gate report, plus the systems, interfaces, scope, staffing and commercial baseline.
solution-brief.outputs: A validated solution graph rendered as a Solution Brief, build reference or field guide, or a Technical Readiness Memo when evidence is insufficient.
solution-brief.example: Explain whether this solution can be delivered, including systems, interfaces, risks and decisions.
solution-brief.expect: It starts from a validated evidence ledger and gate report, then judges whether the solution is deliverable and builds a graph that a script validates before any page is drafted. If the evidence gate is Insufficient it stops at a short Technical Readiness Memo, and it does not approve margin, rates or commercial terms.
solution-brief.requires: A validated evidence ledger and gate report from the evidence-core step, and Python 3; field guide mode also needs Node.js and Playwright for its browser check.

sow.what: Draft a statement of work from confirmed scope.
sow.when: A fixed-scope, adaptive, or assessment agreement needs drafting.
sow.inputs: The confirmed quote model and the project’s approved contract and brand profiles.
sow.outputs: A reconciled Word document and checks against the selected scope and terms.
sow.example: Draft the selected SOW variant from this confirmed quote and approved contract profile.
sow.expect: It reads one confirmed quote revision, picks the SOW variant from the engagement shape, and renders a .docx only after the hours and revenue tie out. A figure that does not reconcile stops the build and is returned to the quote owner, missing values stay visible as flagged fields, and the document is never treated as approved or sent.

sow-quality.what: Review a statement of work and its obligations.
sow-quality.when: A SOW or contractual scope needs a quality review.
sow-quality.inputs: The draft agreement, confirmed scope, estimate, and controlling terms.
sow-quality.outputs: Findings or revisions addressing ambiguity, duplication, and scope consistency.
sow-quality.example: Review this SOW for ambiguous obligations and inconsistencies with the agreed scope.
sow-quality.expect: It reads the whole SOW with its quote and template, runs a scan for repeated mechanics, then fixes structure and cross-references and re-scans. It flags numbers that do not trace to the pricing source instead of changing them, and the edited document stays unapproved.
sow-quality.requires: The SOW as a .docx or text with its controlling quote, and Python 3 for the scan script.

spec-writer.what: Specify detailed UI, API, and data behavior.
spec-writer.when: A feature specification needs implementation detail.
spec-writer.inputs: The current implementation, user flows, interfaces, data, and constraints.
spec-writer.outputs: A detailed specification with states, persistence, interfaces, and acceptance checks.
spec-writer.example: Specify the UI states, API contracts, and data changes for this feature.
spec-writer.expect: It reads the project instructions and relevant code first, then writes only the sections the feature needs: states, data changes, endpoints, a file manifest and executable acceptance checks. It keeps planned verification separate from commands that actually ran and does not invent owners, dates or approvals.

sprint-planning.what: Plan one sprint against measured team capacity.
sprint-planning.when: A team is about to commit to a sprint, or sprints keep missing their goal.
sprint-planning.inputs: Team availability, the backlog-refinement readiness report, the RAID log, recent velocity and the definition of done.
sprint-planning.outputs: A sprint plan with a goal, capacity, commit and stretch work, owned dependencies and a gate result.
sprint-planning.example: Plan sprint 5 for a team of four with one person out for three days.
sprint-planning.expect: It asks for capacity, velocity, the definition of done and the readiness report, then drafts a sprint goal and a commit and stretch split and runs a gate script. The gate exits 1 on over-capacity or not-ready commitments, and the plan is a proposal because the team decides the commitment and the tracker is never changed.
sprint-planning.requires: Python 3 for the gate script, plus a readiness report from backlog refinement and a RAID log if you want the gate to check them.

sticker-art-direction.what: Develop and critique typography-led sticker designs.
sticker-art-direction.when: A sticker concept needs composition, type exploration, or print-scale review.
sticker-art-direction.inputs: The concept, collection references, source assets, and production constraints.
sticker-art-direction.outputs: Design directions, refined compositions, and print-scale proofs.
sticker-art-direction.example: Develop distinct type treatments for this sticker concept and review them at print scale.
sticker-art-direction.expect: It works from your phrase and any brief, looks at documented references, and shows structurally different compositions rather than font swaps. It auditions the actual words in real font files, critiques at print scale, and will not reproduce a recognizable existing design or authorize publication.

sticker-sheets.what: Lay out the user’s sticker designs for Cricut printing.
sticker-sheets.when: Her PNG designs need exact-count Print Then Cut sheets.
sticker-sheets.inputs: The designs, requested sizes and counts, and the user’s project generator.
sticker-sheets.outputs: Generated sheets and layout checks before a physical print test.
sticker-sheets.example: Lay out these PNGs in the requested sizes and counts using my current sheet generator.
sticker-sheets.reuseNote: Use the caller’s explicitly supplied or authorized sources, configuration, profile and destination. No personal identity or standing permissions transfer with the workflow.
sticker-sheets.expect: It finds the project's sheet generator, reads its help, and confirms paper size separately from the cut area before laying out your PNGs. It runs with branding off unless you ask for a maker mark, then checks the manifest, contact sheet, DPI and every requested count, reporting any skipped duplicates.
sticker-sheets.requires: The project's sheet generator script and the supplied PNG designs; if the generator is unavailable it asks for it instead of guessing.

system-design.what: Explore a system or service design.
system-design.when: A working architecture or technical trade-off discussion is needed.
system-design.inputs: The problem, requirements, constraints, scale, and existing system context.
system-design.outputs: A working design covering components, data, interfaces, and trade-offs.
system-design.example: Explore a working design for this service, including its data flow and trade-offs.
system-design.expect: It states its assumptions, then walks requirements, components, data model, APIs, scaling and trade-offs, leading with a recommended design. It marks assumed scale or latency figures as assumed instead of inventing them, and points you to the formal architecture mode if you need a sourced reference.

team-onboarding.what: Plan a role’s first 30, 60, and 90 days.
team-onboarding.when: A new starter or team transition needs a structured ramp.
team-onboarding.inputs: The role, success criteria, mentors, existing materials, access, and time budget.
team-onboarding.outputs: A role-specific onboarding plan with learning, contribution, and feedback milestones.
team-onboarding.example: Create a 30/60/90-day plan for this role using the team’s mentoring and access constraints.
team-onboarding.expect: It asks for the role, existing docs, who will mentor, the access needed and how much team time is available, then produces a pre-day-1 checklist, day-1 schedule, reading list, 30/60/90 milestones, buddy guide and retrospective template. It delivers in chat unless you ask for a file.

transcript-ingestion.what: Preserve and index a meeting transcript.
transcript-ingestion.when: A transcript or recording export needs a durable project record.
transcript-ingestion.inputs: The original transcript and confirmed client, opportunity, or engagement identity.
transcript-ingestion.outputs: A preserved source, normalized transcript, and indexed meeting record.
transcript-ingestion.example: Preserve and index this transcript under its confirmed opportunity and meeting identity.
transcript-ingestion.expect: It confirms the client and an opportunity or engagement ID before filing and stops if the meeting could belong to more than one. It keeps the raw transcript untouched, writes a normalized copy and index entry, and proposes claims with locators that go through the evidence step rather than being promoted directly.
transcript-ingestion.requires: A transcript file (Markdown, text or VTT), a confirmed client and opp- or eng- context ID, and Python 3 for the normalizer on a local machine.

uat-validation.what: Trace tests to requirements, track UAT and assemble the go or no-go evidence.
uat-validation.when: Testing starts, or someone asks for test scripts, coverage or whether the release is ready.
uat-validation.inputs: The requirements workbook, the Test Plan, the SOW acceptance section, build status and reported test results.
uat-validation.outputs: Traced test scripts, a defect log, a UAT tracker with coverage, and a go or no-go pack with an empty decision block.
uat-validation.example: Build the test scripts and traceability check from this requirements workbook.
uat-validation.expect: It finds the requirements workbook, Test Plan and SOW acceptance language first and stops with a gap memo if one is missing.
